module_title: CIRP Mechanics, Moratorium, and Voting Thresholds
introduction: This intermediate tier drives into the operational legal mechanics of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). It analyzes who can trigger the code, the devastating legal freeze of the Moratorium, the absolute powers of the Committee of Creditors (CoC), and special MSME resolution paths.

core_concepts.title: Triggering CIRP: Section 7 vs. Section 9 vs. Section 10
core_concepts.description:
The CIRP can be initiated by three distinct entities once a default crosses ₹1 Crore:
- Section 7: Initiated by a **Financial Creditor**. They only need to prove the existence of a default via records from an Information Utility.
- Section 9: Initiated by an **Operational Creditor**. Crucially, they must first serve a mandatory 10-day demand notice under Section 8. If the debtor proves a 'pre-existing dispute' before the notice, the petition must be dismissed.
- Section 10: Initiated by the **Corporate Debtor** themselves to voluntarily enter insolvency.

core_concepts.title: The Moratorium (Section 14)
core_concepts.description:
Upon admitting a CIRP petition, the NCLT declares a mandatory Moratorium. 
- The Freeze: It creates a legal shield prohibiting: (1) the institution or continuation of suits/execution of decrees against the debtor, (2) transferring or alienating any assets, and (3) enforcing any security interest (SARFAESI actions are frozen). 
- Purpose: To preserve the debtor's asset corpus as a 'going concern' while a resolution plan is designed.

core_concepts.title: The Committee of Creditors (CoC) & Voting Thresholds
core_concepts.description:
Once CIRP begins, the Resolution Professional forms the CoC, comprising **only Financial Creditors** (Operational Creditors have no voting power in the CoC, though they can attend if their debt is >= 10% of total debt).
- Voting Shares: Calculated based on the value of the financial debt owed.
- Core Thresholds: (1) **66% voting majority** is required for critical decisions like approving a Resolution Plan or replacing the Resolution Professional. (2) **51% voting majority** for routine administrative decisions. (3) **90% voting majority** to completely withdraw a CIRP application under Section 12A.

core_concepts.title: Pre-Packaged Insolvency (PPIRP) for MSMEs (Section 54A)
core_concepts.description:
Introduced via amendment to provide a faster, cheaper resolution for MSMEs.
- Mechanism: It is a hybrid 'pre-pack' where the debtor and financial creditors informally agree on a resolution plan *before* approaching the NCLT. Unlike standard CIRP, management stays with the MSME promoters during the process ('Debtor-in-Possession'), minimizing business disruption.

important_entities.name: The CIRP Statutory Timeline (Section 12)
important_entities.significance: The IBC mandates that CIRP must be completed within **180 days** from admission. The NCLT can grant a single extension of up to 90 days. However, the total resolution period, including any litigation delays or extensions, **must mandatorily be completed within 330 days**, failing which the company automatically enters Liquidation.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In an operational creditor's petition under Section 9, if the corporate debtor can show that a dispute regarding the quality of goods or breach of contract existed *before* the Section 8 demand notice was received, the NCLT has **no choice but to reject the petition**. NCLT cannot adjudicate complex contractual breaches; it only checks for an undisputed default.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: 90 to Exit, 66 to Fix, 51 to Run
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: 90% vote to withdraw (12A), 66% vote to approve a plan/replace RP, 51% vote for routine administrative matters.

exam_strategy_tips: If a problem-based exam scenario involves homebuyers, remember that following the statutory amendments and the *Chitra Sharma* judgment, **Homebuyers are legally classified as Financial Creditors** (allottees under a real estate project) and have a seat in the CoC.
